A stimulus set is usually described without being shared. The methods section
says the words were matched on length and frequency, and the set itself, the
criteria that produced it and the code that applied them are not recoverable from
the paper. `lexsync` treats the set as an artefact in its own right. The selection
and the trial order are deterministic, the R and Python engines produce the same
artefacts from the same input, and each run emits a provenance record with the
checksums needed to verify it.

This vignette covers the guarantee and its limits, the mechanisms that achieve
it, the continuous-integration test that checks it and the two records a run
writes.

```{r setup}
library(lexsync)
schema <- yaml::read_yaml(
  system.file("extdata", "schema.yaml", package = "lexsync")
)
lex <- load_lexicon(
  system.file("extdata", "en_example.csv", package = "lexsync"),
  schema, language = "english"
)
pool <- build_pool(lex, list(length = c(3, 7), frequency = c(3.8, 7.0)))

design <- list(
  name = "vignette_repro", language = "english", n_per_condition = 15,
  conditions = list(
    list(name = "high", define_by = list(frequency = c(5.2, 7.0))),
    list(name = "low",  define_by = list(frequency = c(3.8, 4.4)))
  ),
  match_on = list("length", "n_density", "old20"),
  counterbalance = list(lists = 1)
)
```

## What is guaranteed

Given the same lexicon and the same design, the R and Python engines produce
byte-identical stimuli under the `standardised_euclidean` and `joint` matching
methods, under continuous selection and under both pseudoword generators. The
guarantee covers which items are chosen, how they are paired and the order they
are presented in, so the generated experiments are byte-identical in full. For
every worked design, the PsychoPy script, the OpenSesame file, the jsPsych page
and the three CSV tables that the PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments read are
byte-identical across the engines. The only exceptions are the `mahalanobis` and
`optimal` matching methods.

'Byte-identical' is meant literally, and the artefacts are compared as bytes. A
comparison of parsed values would treat `1` and `1.0`, `FALSE` and `False`, or
`9e-4` and `0.0009` as equal although the files differ.

Means need the same care, since two engines that sum in different orders, one
pairwise and one not, can report means that differ in the last decimal. Every sum
in the package therefore goes through one compensated-summation algorithm written
out in both engines, and the mean, variance and standard deviation are built on
it. The two implementations of that algorithm agree because IEEE-754 requires
addition and subtraction to be correctly rounded. The median sorts and takes the
middle value, or the plain-double average of the two middle values when the count
is even. It avoids `stats::median()`, which uses a long-double accumulator by way
of `mean()`.

Two files are outside the guarantee because each records the engine that produced
it. The materials datasheet names its engine and that engine's package versions,
and the run log adds wall-clock timestamps. Their contents are compared field by
field instead.

Within one engine, selection is a pure function of its input.

```{r determinism}
a <- match_stimuli(pool, design, schema)
b <- match_stimuli(pool, design, schema)
identical(a, b)
```

Repeated calls agree because nothing in the selection path consults a random
number generator and because every operation that could depend on the ambient
environment has been made independent of it. The Python engine agrees as well,
although the two implementations share no code.

## How byte-identical output is achieved

Cross-engine identity rests on a set of mechanisms, each of which removes one way
in which the engines could otherwise differ.

There is no random number generator anywhere in the package. The obvious way to
choose 15 items from 700 is to sample them, and `lexsync` never does. The anchor
condition is chosen by an even spread across its sorted subpool, taking positions
along the whole range, and every later item is determined by a distance. A seeded
generator would not help, because R's Mersenne-Twister stream and NumPy's stream
differ. The same seed gives different draws, so any sampling step would break
parity. Trial order is also decided without a generator, by the shuffle described
below.

```{r even-spread}
anchor_pool <- pool[pool$frequency >= 5.2 & pool$frequency <= 7.0, ]
anchor_pool <- anchor_pool[
  order(anchor_pool$frequency, anchor_pool$word, method = "radix"),
]
idx <- unique(round(seq(1, nrow(anchor_pool), length.out = 15)))
idx
```

The spread is `seq()` over the row positions, rounded to integers. Both engines
compute the same positions from the same row count with the same expression,
`unique(round(seq(...)))`, and the rounding rule is written out in both. The
`unique()` matters when the pool is smaller than the requested n and the rounding
produces a repeated index.

Sorting is by byte order everywhere. R's default string sort is locale-collated.
A French locale, a C locale and a Windows locale can order the same words
differently, and any of those orders would differ from Python's, which sorts by
code point. Every sort on the selection path therefore passes `method = "radix"`,
which sorts by bytes.

```{r radix}
words <- c("zebra", "Apple", "apple", "Zebra")
sort(words, method = "radix")
```

Uppercase sorts before lowercase because that is the byte order, and Python's
`sorted()` gives the same result. A locale-collated sort would typically
interleave them.

Case folding is made independent of the locale for the same reason.
`load_lexicon()` lower-cases through ICU at the root locale. It avoids
`tolower()`, whose behaviour depends on the C library and the locale and differs
from Python's on Greek final sigma and the dotted Turkish capital I. The locale
is kept out of two more places. Design, schema and registry files are read as
UTF-8 whatever the session's character type, and a file in another encoding is
rejected with an error. The text of every hash key is made UTF-8 before it is
digested, whatever encoding mark it carries. These keys are used for the trial
order, list balancing, jitter and the tie-break between candidates, and a
condition label such as `café` therefore ranks by the same digest in R under the
C locale as in Python.

Frequencies of bigrams and of subsyllabic constituents are accumulated as
integers, so the counts cannot depend on summation order.

Distances are rounded to nine decimal places before the tie-break. Two candidate
words can be at exactly equal distance from an anchor, and the last bits of a
square root can differ between two linear-algebra implementations. If the engines
compared raw doubles, a difference in the fifteenth decimal would make one engine
call a tie and the other not, and they would pick different words. Rounding before
ranking puts both engines on the same side of every comparison that matters.

Rounding creates ties, and both engines break them by the same total order. Under
`tie_break: bytes`, the rule of lexsync 0.1, candidates are ordered by distance,
then by the word's bytes, then by its integer `id`. The matcher's comparison is
reproduced here on three imaginary candidates.

```{r tie-break}
distance <- c(0.5, 0.5, 0.2)
word     <- c("beta", "alpha", "gamma")
id       <- c(1L, 2L, 3L)
word[order(distance, word, id, method = "radix")]
```

`gamma` wins on distance. `alpha` and `beta` are tied on distance to the ninth
decimal, and the word's bytes settle the tie in the same way in both engines.
Since `word` is unique within a lexicon, the order is total and there is always
exactly one winner.

Under `tie_break: hash`, the default, the word's tie key takes the place of its
bytes. The tie key is the hexadecimal SHA-256 of `lexsync-tie-v1|` followed by
the word. Both engines compute the key from the same UTF-8 bytes and sort it the
same way. The code below orders four candidates tied on distance by each rule.

```{r tie-break-hash}
tied <- c("bat", "cat", "dog", "eel")
key <- vapply(paste0("lexsync-tie-v1|", tied), digest::digest, character(1),
              algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE, USE.NAMES = FALSE)
data.frame(bytes = tied[order(tied, method = "radix")],
           hash = tied[order(key, method = "radix")])
```

Either rule is a total order that the two engines compute identically, so either
keeps the guarantee. The setting `matching.tie_break` chooses between them.
`bytes` reproduces the selections of lexsync 0.1. `hash` stops a condition
decided by ties from filling with early-alphabet words, which the matching
vignette measures. The salt is fixed and independent of the seed, which keys the
trial order. A tie key built on the seed would change the items whenever a
cohort's order was re-randomised, and would let a researcher choose among equally
matched sets by re-seeding.

### Trial order: a seeded shuffle without a generator

Trial order cannot come from a seeded generator either, since R's
Mersenne-Twister and NumPy's PCG64 give different permutations from one seed.
Both engines therefore order the trials of a list by a keyed hash. Each row is
ranked by the SHA-256 digest of `seed|replicate|list|set|condition`, a tuple that
identifies the trial uniquely under either counterbalancing recipe. Distinct
inputs to SHA-256 behave as independent uniform draws, so sorting the rows by
their digests realises a seeded random permutation. Because a digest is a pure
function of its input, the permutation is a pure function of the design. Both
engines give the same bytes on any platform, there is no generator state to save
or restore, and a different seed gives a different order. The implementation is
`.shuffle_deterministic()` in `R/counterbalancing.R`, mirrored in the Python
engine's `counterbalancing.py`.

```{r trial-order}
stim <- counterbalance(match_stimuli(pool, design, schema), design, schema)
head(stim[, c("trial", "condition", "word")], 4)
same <- counterbalance(match_stimuli(pool, design, schema), design, schema)
identical(stim$trial, same$trial)
```

The order is random in the sense a study needs, with no systematic relation
between an item's properties and its position. Counterbalancing does not touch the
random number generator, since nothing in the package consults one. Calling it
from a longer script therefore cannot disturb the stream your own code is drawing
from.

## The CSV input contract

Both engines read a lexicon, a norm table, a supplied pool or an item table by
one rule. Each engine reads every cell as text and converts it itself, because
readr and pandas guess types by different heuristics. Left to them, a padded
category or a column of `T` and `F` would be read differently by the two engines.

Header names and cells are trimmed of spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line
feeds. After trimming, an empty cell and `NA`, quoted or not, are missing, and
every other word is a value. A column is numeric only when every value is a plain
decimal number, with an optional sign, point and exponent and no thousands
separators, so `1,000` is text. It is logical only when every value is TRUE or
FALSE in upper, lower or title case, so `T` and `F` stay text. Any other column
is text, a column of dates included. Every row counts towards the type. The
columns a paradigm presents, and an item table's `item` and `condition`, are
always text. A header that names a column twice is rejected with an error, and an
empty header cell is named by its position (`...3`).

The numbers themselves are parsed to the same double in both engines. Python's
`float()` returns the double nearest the decimal. readr's parser and R's
`as.numeric()` can each miss it by one unit in the last place, readr's on
`50.768212762897100` and `as.numeric()` on `0.586135918132`, for instance. This
engine therefore computes every number of up to 15 significant digits, with a
power of ten within 10^22, as one exact integer multiplied or divided by one
exact power of ten. IEEE-754 rounds that single operation correctly, so the
result is Python's double. Every value in the bundled lexica is of that kind.
Any other number is rounded in exact integer arithmetic, which gives Python's
double on every platform. `as.numeric()` is not used there, because it
accumulates the digits in `long double`. Where that type is no wider than a
double, as on Apple Silicon, an emulation of R's parser missed on about one in
ten of the values Python's `repr()` writes for computed doubles. A negative zero
is read as zero, since the two engines would otherwise write it as `-0` and `0`.

## The YAML input contract

A design and the schema are read as YAML 1.1, by `yaml::read_yaml()` here and by
PyYAML in Python, and the two readers resolve a few unquoted values differently.
YAML 1.1 lists `y`, `Y`, `n` and `N` among its booleans, and PyYAML keeps them as
text. lexsync reads them as text in both engines, so `keys: [y, n]` gives the
response keys y and n. Booleans are written `true` and `false`. An unquoted `yes`,
`no`, `on` or `off` is a boolean to both readers as well. A response key that YAML
reads as a boolean is therefore rejected with an error that suggests quoting it. A
norms entry names its join key `join_on`, since a bare `on` is read as true.
`counterbalance.optimise` must be `true` or `false`, and any other value, such as
`n` or `1`, is rejected with an error.

Some known differences remain. PyYAML reads `1:30` as the base-60 number 90,
`1_000` as 1000, `0b101` as 5 and `2026-10-13` as a date, and this engine reads
all four as text. No worked design or schema in the repository holds such a
value. Quote one, or write the number plainly, where a design must read alike in
both engines. This engine also reads a sequence of one value, such as `[true]`,
as that value, while PyYAML keeps a list. `optimise: [true]` or `name: [demo]`
therefore passes here and is rejected in Python, so write a single value without
brackets.

## The Unicode input contract

Word matching, deduplication and the `length` dimension operate on Unicode code
points, and every text key is normalised to Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC).
The words of a lexicon or a supplied pool and both sides of a norm-table or
pair-member join are first trimmed and then lower-cased through ICU at the root
locale. The item id, condition and presented fields of an item table, practice
and filler tables included, and a supplied reference list are normalised as read.
A precomposed character such as `é` and its decomposed counterpart, the base
letter followed by a combining accent, are therefore one character, and a lexicon
that mixes the two conventions holds each word once, in the first row the file
gives it. Unnormalised, the two spellings would be two words of different
lengths, which the matcher could place in opposite conditions of one matched set.
When normalisation rewrites or merges anything, the run log says how many forms
it rewrote and how many duplicates it removed, and the datasheet records the two
counts as `materials_source$input_normalisation`. Input already in NFC, the form
most corpora distribute, produces neither the log entry nor the datasheet field.

Unicode's stability policy fixes the NFC form of every assigned character, so
the two engines can disagree only on a character that one engine's Unicode
version assigns and the other's lacks. R's stringi uses the ICU it bundles or,
on some Linux builds, the system's ICU, which may implement another version, and
Python's `unicodedata` follows the interpreter (Unicode 15.1 in Python 3.13).

The syllable estimator and the pseudoword generators carry a narrower contract
still. Both are orthographic approximations. The estimator is defined for Latin
orthographies, and the generators for alphabetic scripts.
`count_syllables()` decomposes a word (NFD), sets its combining marks aside and
counts the maximal runs of the letters a, e, i, o, u, y, ae (U+00E6), o with
stroke (U+00F8), dotless i (U+0131) and oe (U+0153), so a vowel counts whatever
its accent, in Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Romanian, Turkish and Vietnamese as in
English or Spanish. Hiatus (`idea` counts 2) and the Czech syllabic r and l
(`vlk`, `krk`) stay undercounted. A word holding a character outside the code
points U+0001-U+024F, U+02B0-U+036F, U+1E00-U+1EFF and U+2000-U+206F gets no
estimate. Its `n_syllables` is `NA` in R and NaN in Python, and
`run_pipeline()` stops with an error when a design refers to `n_syllables` while
its pool holds such a word. The test is on code-point ranges, which keeps the two
engines independent of their Unicode tables, and the same stability policy fixes
the decompositions. The pseudoword generators substitute among the letters the
reference words attest, in UTF-8 byte order, so with a Spanish lexicon they use
its accented vowels and `ñ`. They stop with an error on a word in a logographic
script such as Chinese. The worked Chinese design matches on `length`,
`n_density` and `old20` for these reasons.

## File names

Every file a run writes is named after a stem built from the design's `name` and
`language`, which `design_stem()` computes in both engines. The stem keeps ASCII
letters and digits only, so names that differ only outside ASCII would share it.
Two designs with Chinese names, both in `chinese`, would write the same files, the
second overwriting the first. Whenever the name or the language holds a non-ASCII
character, the stem therefore ends in an underscore and the first eight
hexadecimal digits of the SHA-256 of the NFC-normalised text `name|language`, such
as `chinese_14aadfa7`. A name and language with no ASCII letter or digit get
those eight digits alone. Normalising to NFC here keeps a precomposed and a
decomposed spelling of one name on one stem. Names in plain ASCII are unaffected.
`run_all()` also computes every design's stem before it runs any, and stops with
an error if two designs would write the same files, such as `en-lexdec` and
`en_lexdec`.

## The documented exceptions

Under `mahalanobis` and `optimal`, the two engines compute equivalent quantities
but need not select the same items.

`mahalanobis` needs the inverse of the pool's correlation matrix. A matrix
inverse is computed by LAPACK, and R's LAPACK is not necessarily the one NumPy is
built against. The two may differ in blocking, in vectorisation and in the order
they accumulate sums. The results agree to well within any tolerance you would
care about but need not agree in their last bits. The rounding that keeps the
Euclidean path identical does not help here, because the distance is a function
of a matrix whose entries already differ below the rounding threshold, so the
rounding can go either way.

`optimal` solves a linear assignment problem. Where several assignments have the
same total cost, which one a solver returns is an implementation detail of the
solver, and R's `clue::solve_LSAP()` and SciPy's implementation resolve those ties
differently. Both return an optimal assignment. They need not return the
same one.

Neither difference is a bug. Guaranteeing these methods would mean writing a
bit-exact matrix inverse and a tie-canonical assignment solver in both languages,
a large amount of numerical code to maintain for a modest gain. The chosen
trade-off is to keep a byte-identical method as the default, document the
exception and record it per run. The same trade-off shapes the roadmap. A
covariance-aware distance might well be the better default, and it stays optional
because it cannot carry the guarantee.

```{r cross-engine}
maha <- design
maha$matching <- list(method = "mahalanobis")
maha_stim <- match_stimuli(pool, maha, schema)
maha_ds <- build_datasheet(
  maha, schema, NULL, maha_stim,
  system.file("extdata", "en_example.csv", package = "lexsync"),
  list(stimuli = NA_character_), schema$seed
)
maha_ds$selection$cross_engine
```

Every datasheet carries this field, so a reader of the record does not have to
know the rule. It reads `byte-identical` for `standardised_euclidean` and
`joint`, and `approximate (platform linear algebra)` for `mahalanobis` and
`optimal`. The generated methods paragraph adds a sentence stating the caveat in
prose when it applies.

Almost everything on the path to a compared artefact is built from operations
that IEEE-754 either mandates to be correctly rounded or makes exact, so the
engines agree by construction rather than by measurement. That argument does not
cover the Student t quantile and distribution behind the confidence interval and
the TOST *p*-value. They come from `stats::qt` and `stats::pt` in R and from
SciPy's implementation in Python, two independent implementations that were
measured to disagree by up to about 1e-12 over the range these reports use. The
published values are rounded to three and four decimal places, which leaves
margins of 5e-4 and 5e-5. The comparisons files therefore still come out
byte-identical, and these values are not among the documented exceptions. The
guarantee there rests on a margin of some seven orders of magnitude rather than on
construction, and the reported precision should not be widened without checking
that margin first.

`normalise_lexicon()` has the same kind of step. Zipf = log10(per million) + 3
calls each engine's own `log10()`, which IEEE-754 does not require to be correctly
rounded. A value whose scaled Zipf lies within one unit in the last place of a
rounding boundary could therefore round to different three-place values in the
two engines. The function counts the values that lie within 1e-9 of a boundary,
and the count is expected to be 0. A run over a lexicon carrying
`freq_permillion` records it as `materials_source$zipf_derivation` in its
datasheet and in its run log. A registry entry's `derived` file, a lexicon
normalised once and checksummed, lets both engines read the same bytes and
involves no such step.

## The parity test

The parity gate in continuous integration runs the R pipeline over the worked
designs, regenerates each with the Python engine and compares the two. The
designs cover both engines' matching methods, continuous selection, both
pseudoword generators, resampling, priming and self-paced reading, three
languages including a logographic script, and three reproductions of published
designs.

The comparison is on identity columns. For a design that selects its own items,
they are the word or target, the condition and the `set` index, and for one that
reads an item table, they are the list, the `set` index, the condition and the
item's presented fields. A case adds the columns it exists to check: `list` for
balanced lists, `replicate` for resampled sets, `trial` for practice and filler
blocks, the realised `prime_ms` and `iti_ms` for jittered timing, the joined member
and pair columns for the pair-keyed design, the looked-up dimensions for a
supplied pool, `prime_type` for the masked-priming reproduction and `answer` for
categorisation. `set` is included because, without it, the engines could select
the same items, pair them differently and still pass. The test then checks every
other shared column, so the `trial` position and the dimensions each engine
computes at run time (`n_density`, `old20`, `n_syllables`, `bigram_freq`) must
also agree.

Three details keep the gate from passing vacuously. The test skips when the R
reference output is absent, since the Python package can be installed on its
own. CI sets `LEXSYNC_REQUIRE_PARITY=1` to turn those skips into failures, so a
job meant to run both engines cannot pass by quietly skipping. The R references
are regenerated and then checked with `git diff --exit-code`, so an R-engine
regression fails the build. Without that step, the comparison would run against a
stale snapshot that the regression matches. The R suite is also run once from
the source tree with a check that nothing skipped, because the repository-coupled
tests skip silently when run from an installed copy.

The worked designs have clean inputs: every cell is in NFC, none is padded and
the norms cover every word. The gate therefore never runs the code that handles
padded fields, missing values or unusual YAML, and a defect that both engines
share would pass it. The twin-edge cases test that code. Each is a folder under
`parity/twin_edge/` at the repository root, holding a small `design.yaml`, its
inputs, an optional `schema.yaml` and an `expect.yaml` that states the expected
outcome. Input paths are relative to the folder. An artefacts case keeps the
files the design must produce, byte for byte, in `expected/`, and may assert
values in the datasheet. A refusal case gives a substring of the error the design
must raise.

The R suite's `test-twin-edge.R` and the Python suite's `test_twin_edge.py` each
check their own engine against every case. CI also runs
`tools/compare_engines.py`, which compares the two engines on the same cases and
repeats the whole-tree comparison on any machine. To add a case, create its
folder with `design.yaml` and `expect.yaml` and write `expected/` with
`python tools/twin_edge.py --update <case>`. Read the files it writes to confirm
they are right, then run the R suite, which checks that the R engine writes the
same bytes. A fix for an input defect adds its case in the same commit, so that
no commit leaves the gate failing.

## The materials datasheet

Each run emits a datasheet in two forms, a JSON record for machines and a
Markdown rendering for people. It exists because the reproducibility literature
in linguistics keeps finding the same gap. Materials are described but rarely
deposited in a form that permits reuse or verification (Bochynska et al., 2023),
and the degrees of freedom in preparing them are large enough to matter
(Roettger, 2019). A datasheet is the FAIR-style record of one selection
(Wilkinson et al., 2016).

```{r datasheet}
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "lexsync_repro")
dir.create(out, showWarnings = FALSE)
report <- match_report(
  stim, c("frequency", "length", "n_density", "old20"), schema
)
stim_path <- file.path(out, "stimuli.csv")
write.csv(stim, stim_path, row.names = FALSE)

ds <- build_datasheet(
  design, schema, report, stim,
  source_path = system.file("extdata", "en_example.csv", package = "lexsync"),
  artifacts = list(stimuli = stim_path),
  seed = schema$seed,
  candidate_pool = lapply(design$conditions, function(cnd)
    list(
      condition = cnd$name,
      n_candidates = nrow(build_pool(pool, cnd$define_by))
    ))
)
names(ds)
```

The record answers the questions a sceptical reader would ask. Where the words
came from, and whether this is the same file, is settled by `materials_source`,
which carries the path and its SHA-256. What was applied is recorded in
`selection`, covering the method, the matched dimensions and the tolerance
windows as resolved by merging the design's overrides onto the schema's defaults.
The rule that broke exact ties is there too, as `tie_break`, with its salt under
`hash`.

What the selection achieved is in `realised_control`, as the effect sizes,
intervals, variance ratios and TOST verdicts for every pair of conditions, each
row naming its pair in `condition` and `reference`, giving the raw difference as
`mean_diff` and the dimension's role. What it could have chosen instead is in
`candidate_pool`, which records how many items satisfied each condition before
matching. A candidate missing a matched dimension satisfies its condition but
cannot be matched. Such candidates are counted in `incomplete_dropped`, present
only when a condition lost any, and the methods paragraph leaves them out of its
count of eligible candidates.

How the items were assigned to lists is in `counterbalancing`. It gives the
recipe that ran, the lists the stimuli table holds and the trials each list gives
each condition, and it says whether a Latin-square rotation is complete. How many
items there are is in `items`, whose `n_per_condition_realised` counts the items
each condition holds, per replicate for resampled sets. The request the selector
applied is `design$n_per_condition`, the selector's default when the design gives
none.

The record keeps each statistic as the comparisons report rounded it, to three
places and the TOST *p* to four. The Markdown rendering and the methods paragraph
show them at two or three places and the TOST *p* at four. The rounding is done
from that record by lexsync's own formatter, half away from zero, so both engines
print the same digits. A *d* of 0.1649 is stored as 0.165 and is therefore shown
as 0.17.

```{r checksums}
ds$materials_source$sha256
str(ds$selection$tolerance_k)
do.call(rbind, lapply(ds$selection$candidate_pool, as.data.frame))
```

The candidate-pool counts show that the high condition here was drawn from fewer
than a hundred eligible words and the low condition from several hundred.
Choosing 15 items from a large candidate set invites the concern that a selection
could be steered towards almost any result, whereas a condition with barely more
candidates than items had little freedom to be steered. Recording the counts,
alongside the fact that the selection is deterministic and blind to any outcome
measure, lets a reader judge that risk.

The resolved windows include a `frequency` entry, although this design matches
on the three orthographic dimensions only. The record reports the windows as
resolved from the schema and the design, and a window is applied only to a
dimension named in `match_on`.

```{r versions}
str(ds$reproducibility)
```

The reproducibility block records the seed and the versions of the engine and its
dependencies, since a bug fix in a dependency can change a selection and the
record should say which versions produced this one.

### The methods paragraph and the pre-registration template

`methods_paragraph()` turns the datasheet into prose. Generating the text removes
a common source of error, a methods section transcribed by hand from numbers on a
screen.

```{r methods-paragraph}
cat(strwrap(methods_paragraph(ds), width = 76), sep = "\n")
```

The paragraph is generated from the record, so it cannot disagree with the
stimuli. It states the number of items each condition holds and the
candidate-pool size, and it adds the cross-engine caveat when the design's method
warrants it. It describes the realised control before it tests it, since tests on
a selected set concern a closed population (Sassenhagen & Alday, 2016). It gives
the largest difference on any matched dimension, in that dimension's unit, with
*d* and its interval, and only then the two one-sided tests, with the number of
matched comparisons they supported. It then names, largest first, up to five
comparisons of a dimension the design did not control whose |*d*| exceeds the
equivalence bound. The report here covers only the matched dimensions and
frequency, which defines the conditions, so there is none to name.

This run shows why the order matters, and why the paragraph should be read and
adapted before use. The demonstration matches only 15 items per condition. At a
bound of 0.5 SD and an alpha of .05, no dimension that varies can pass the tests
with fewer than 23 items per condition, however well it is matched. The paragraph
says so, and a failed test is then not mistaken for a failed match. The matching
vignette warns against overlooking this dependence on set size. A study, unlike
this demonstration, would either match enough items or report the control by the
differences the paragraph describes.

`write_datasheet()` writes both forms, and the Markdown rendering carries a
pre-registration skeleton with its materials section already filled in.

```{r write-datasheet}
paths <- write_datasheet(
  ds, file.path(out, "datasheet.json"), file.path(out, "datasheet.md")
)
md <- readLines(file.path(out, "datasheet.md"))
grep("^#", md, value = TRUE)
```

The sections left blank are the hypotheses, the sampling plan and the inference
criteria, which no tool can fill. The analysis plan is the exception and comes
with a suggested model.

```{r analysis}
ds$analysis$suggested_model
```

The model crosses random effects for subjects and items because items are a sample
of the language rather than the population of interest. An analysis treating
them as fixed generalises only to the words that were used (Clark, 1973; Yarkoni,
2022). The matched dimensions enter as centred covariates, computed from the
stimuli file's own columns, because matching leaves residual differences and
Sassenhagen and Alday (2016) recommend adjusting for potential confounds. A
structure is maximal only when every effect that varies within subjects or items
has a random slope there (Barr et al., 2013). These covariates have none, so the
accompanying note describes the slopes the model has. The note also advises
simplifying a model that is singular or fails to converge (Matuschek et al.,
2017). The suggested model is a starting point for a design of this shape.

## The run log

Alongside the datasheet, which records what a run produced, the run log records
what the run did.

```{r run-log}
log <- new_run_log(
  "vignette_repro",
  meta = list(seed = schema$seed, language = "english")
)
log <- log_step(
  log,
  sprintf("lexicon loaded: %d words", nrow(lex)),
  list(words = nrow(lex))
)
log <- log_step(log, sprintf("pool after filters: %d words", nrow(pool)))
log <- log_artefact(log, stim_path, rows = nrow(stim))
log_md <- write_run_log(log, file.path(out, "run_log.md"),
                        file.path(out, "run_log.jsonl"))
cat(readLines(log_md), sep = "\n")
```

The pipeline builds this log as it goes, recording each stage with its parameters,
the equivalence verdict on every dimension, any balance warning and an entry per
file written with its MD5. The experiments' loop and text tables are among them,
and the stimuli and report tables are logged with their row counts too. A design
or schema key that lexsync does not read is noted there as well, since it changed
nothing about the run.

A Markdown log and a JSON Lines log are emitted. The Markdown log alone carries
the run metadata, such as the seed and the schema path, and the JSON Lines log
holds the steps, one object per line, so that a run can be checked by a script.
The MD5 here is a content fingerprint for detecting changes between runs, whereas
the datasheet's SHA-256 is the stronger one that belongs in a permanent record.

## Reproducing a run

The pipeline does all of the above in one call. `run_pipeline()` on a design
configuration is the reproducible unit, and it writes the stimuli, the reports,
the three experiments, the datasheet and the log. Sharing the design file and the
corpus is then enough for someone else to regenerate the materials and verify the
checksums in either language.

Two habits keep a run reproducible. Pin the corpus, since a selection is only
reproducible against a fixed lexicon. For this reason, the bundled corpora are a
checksummed snapshot, and the `wordfreq` connector draws on a package frozen in
2024, whose data is a stable snapshot of usage through roughly 2021. Where
cross-engine reproducibility matters, prefer `standardised_euclidean`, the
default, or `joint`, since they are the methods that carry the guarantee.

A reproducible lexicon is not a screened one. The repository's
`corpora/derived/en.csv`, `es.csv` and `zh.csv` hold the most frequent forms
`wordfreq` returns, so they include proper names, acronyms and other forms that are
not words of the language, and N and OLD20 are computed over them. Their share
differs between frequency bands, which can confound a frequency contrast.
`corpora/derived/en_v2.csv` marks such forms in the English lexicon and counts N
and OLD20 among the others only. The package's English example holds only forms
that `en_v2.csv` leaves unmarked, while its Spanish and Chinese examples are slices
of `es.csv` and `zh.csv` and are not screened. [What the derived lexica
contain](https://github.com/pablobernabeu/lexsync/blob/main/corpora/ATTRIBUTION.md#what-the-derived-lexica-contain)
says what to check in a selection.
